Chapter 7: The Freedom of Letting Go of “Shoulds”
You know, there’s a quiet kind of pressure that hides in the word “should.” It slips into our thoughts and conversations, guiding our choices—sometimes without us even realizing it. Think about all those inner voices: “I should be more successful.” “I should be happier.” “I should do what’s expected of me.” These “shoulds” can feel like an invisible cage, quietly telling us how we’re supposed to live.
Picture this: a woman in her thirties walks into therapy, completely worn down by the weight of expectations. She’s done everything she was supposed to—built her career, gotten married, bought a house—but still feels a strange emptiness inside. As she talks through her life, she lists all the things she “should” want, but you can hear it in her voice... there’s no spark. Her therapist gently encourages her to notice the difference between what she truly wants and what she’s been told she should want.
At first, letting go of all those “shoulds” feels risky. What if she lets her parents down? What if she doesn’t measure up to her own expectations? But as she digs deeper, she starts to see just how much her life has been shaped by other people’s values. And suddenly, it becomes clear: chasing approval has cost her real happiness.
Most of the time, we don’t even notice how “should” shapes our decisions. It’s a habit we pick up early on—reinforced by family, culture, even society. In therapy, the invitation is simple but powerful: start questioning those assumptions. Whose voice is really guiding your choices?
Take another example—a man brought up to believe vulnerability equals weakness. He tells himself he “should” always be strong, “should” have everything under control. But as he slowly challenges these beliefs, he finds a new kind of strength: the courage to be honest about what he’s going through. Letting go of “shoulds” isn’t about shirking responsibility—it’s about embracing who you really are.
Here’s the thing: letting go of “shoulds” isn’t just a one-time decision. It’s a process. It means noticing when those old patterns pop up, and choosing to act from self-awareness instead of obligation. It’s about learning to trust your own desires, even if they don’t match what everyone else expects.
Imagine a young artist, feeling crushed by the pressure to pick a “practical” career. Eventually, she finds the courage to follow her passion. Sure, she faces criticism and doubt, but she also discovers a fulfillment she’d never known before. Having the freedom to choose her own path fills her with new energy and purpose.
In therapy, people learn something life-changing: their worth isn’t tied to whether they meet other people’s standards. They start to see that it’s possible to live in line with their own values, and to make choices that reflect who they really are—not who they’re supposed to be. It’s not always easy—there’s fear, uncertainty, and sometimes pushback. But the rewards? Integrity, genuine self-respect, and a deep sense of satisfaction.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the freedom to let go of “shoulds” is the freedom to live your own life. It’s the permission to be imperfect, to make mistakes, and to keep growing. In the end, it’s not about throwing out all expectations—it’s about choosing the ones that truly matter to you.
